passage: Rafael turned up at Ingrid's flat with two suitcases and a parking fine. His lease had ended and his new job didn't start for three weeks. "You're my favourite cousin," he said. Ingrid made up the sofa bed, lent him money for the deposit on his next room, and drove him to the job centre on Monday. On Wednesday he slid the fine across her kitchen table. "You work at the council office. Just make it disappear." Ingrid put down her coffee. "I'll help you pay it bit by bit if you want. I won't make it disappear." "It's nothing to them!" "It's my job, and it's the same rule for everyone who parks there." Rafael sulked through dinner. She passed him the bread anyway. "I love you, and I'm not doing that. Both are true."

qa.q: What did Rafael want Ingrid to do with the parking fine?
qa.a: He wanted her to "just make it disappear" because she works at the council office.

qa.q: What was Ingrid probably feeling when she passed Rafael the bread while he sulked?
qa.a: She was likely firm but still affectionate, wanting him to know her refusal didn't mean she had stopped caring.

qa.q: What made Ingrid's refusal land better than a flat no?
qa.a: She paired it with a real offer, helping him pay bit by bit, and gave a clear reason: the same rule for everyone.

qa.q: How might Rafael see his cousin's refusal once he's settled in his new job?
qa.a: He may realise she gave him a bed, a deposit and a lift, and that the one thing she refused was about fairness, not about him.

grounding: A young adult supports her cousin with a home and money but refuses to cancel his fine, saying plainly that love and honesty can both hold.

passage:
The counter at the municipal office opened at ten, and the queue already curled past the water cooler. Sumit was stamping forms at his desk when Urmila bua appeared at the side door, file in hand. "Beta, just put mine on top. Who will know?"
Sumit stepped out into the corridor with her. "Bua, I spent last Sunday fixing this file with you, and I'll come again if anything's missing. But I can't put it on top."
"For your own bua?"
"That old man in the queue has waited since eight. He's somebody's grandfather."
She laughed despite herself. "Arrey, don't lecture me."
"I'll always help you, Bua. I just won't cheat for you. Now let me get you a chair and some tea."
She took the tea, and a token: number twenty-three.

qa.q: What token number did Urmila bua get?
qa.a: Her token was number twenty-three.

qa.q: Why did Urmila bua laugh despite herself when Sumit mentioned the old man?
qa.a: She seemed to see he had a fair point, even while she was annoyed at being refused 🙂

qa.q: Which of Sumit's choices kept things warm while still keeping the rule?
qa.a: He stepped into the corridor so she wasn't refused in public, reminded her of the Sunday help, and offered a chair and tea while she waited.

qa.q: How might the old man in the queue feel if he saw a relative's file jump to the top?
qa.a: He would likely feel cheated after waiting since eight, and lose trust in the office.

grounding: A young clerk gives his aunt his time and help but refuses to let her skip the queue, saying he will help her but not cheat for her.

passage:
Kamal,
I've transferred the money for your driving course, and I've kept Saturday afternoon free to help you practise for the interview. Please stop thanking me; you're my little brother, that's the job.
About the other thing. You asked me to write an experience letter on my company's letterhead saying you interned with us. I read your message three times. I know how hard these months have been, and I know people say everyone does it. But I won't. If it came out, it would hurt you, my team would be lied to, and someone who really did an internship could lose a seat to a piece of paper.
I can love you and still say no to this. I don't think those two things fight.
Call me tonight. I'm not angry, I promise.
Arohi didi

qa.q: What did Arohi transfer money for?
qa.a: Arohi transferred the money for Kamal's driving course.

qa.q: How does Arohi feel about Kamal's request, judging from reading it three times?
qa.a: She seems troubled and torn, taking his pressure seriously before deciding firmly not to do it.

qa.q: Arohi offered practice time along with the refusal. Why was pairing them a good choice?
qa.a: It shows her support is real and continuing, so the no is about the fake letter, not about him.

qa.q: What would change for other applicants if Arohi had written the letter?
qa.a: Someone who truly did an internship could lose a seat to Kamal's fake paper, which is part of why Arohi refuses.

grounding: A young adult funds and coaches her brother but refuses to write him a false experience letter, saying love and honesty need not fight.

passage: "You want to know why my cousin and I didn't speak for two months, Ganga? Okay. When my uncle's shop burnt down last year, I sent money every month and spent my weekends helping them set up a new stall. My cousin Raju was preparing for his university exams then. I work in the university exam section. One evening he called me and said, 'Didi, just change my practical marks by five. Nobody will notice.' I felt sick. I said, 'I'll pay your coaching fee. I'll sit with you every Sunday. But I will not touch your marks.' He shouted that I cared more about my job than my family. My aunt stopped calling. But I kept going on Sundays. Last month Raju passed on his own and came to my flat with sweets. He said, 'You were right, Manjula didi.' I told him, I love you, and I'm honest. Both are me."

qa.q: What did Raju ask Manjula to change?
qa.a: He asked her to change his practical marks by five.

qa.q: What was Manjula feeling when Raju asked her to change his marks?
qa.a: She felt sick, torn between her love for her cousin and her refusal to be dishonest at work.

qa.q: Which choice by Manjula balanced loyalty and fairness, and why?
qa.a: She refused to change the marks but paid his coaching fee and helped every Sunday, which supported Raju without cheating other students.

qa.q: How did Raju see Manjula's refusal at first, and later?
qa.a: At first he felt betrayed and thought she cared more about her job, but after passing on his own he came with sweets and said she was right.

grounding: A young woman supports relatives with money and time but refuses to change a cousin's marks, saying love and honesty can both be kept.

passage: I'm Shreya, and I share a desk with Nazia in the school admissions office. This March her nephew applied for Class 1 here. The waiting list was long, and her sister called her every evening. Once, from across the room, I heard Nazia say on the phone, "Apa, I will fill his form with you, I will pay the fee, I will pick him up every day if he gets in. But I will not move his name up the list." Her voice was gentle and very firm. Her sister must have said something sharp, because Nazia was quiet for a while and then said, "There are forty other families waiting. They trust this list." I don't know how hard it was for her. She went home early that day. But every Saturday she sat with her nephew practising his letters, and when his name came up fairly in May, she brought laddoos for the whole office.

qa.q: How many other families were waiting on the list, according to Nazia?
qa.a: Forty other families were waiting.

qa.q: What does Nazia's gentle but firm voice suggest about her feelings?
qa.a: It suggests she loves her nephew and sister deeply but is determined not to break the rules, even though it hurts.

qa.q: What does Nazia do to help her nephew without being unfair?
qa.a: She offers to fill his form, pay the fee and pick him up, and she practises letters with him every Saturday, while refusing to change his place on the list.

qa.q: How might the forty other families feel if they knew what Nazia did?
qa.a: They would likely feel reassured and respected, knowing the list was kept fair even when a staff member's own family was waiting.

grounding: A young woman helps her nephew with time and money but declines to move him up an admissions list, keeping both family love and fairness.
